meta.title: How Brazil Voted
meta.description: A dot map of every vote in Brazil's 2026 presidential first round, and where the vote moved since 2022, in every municipality and at every polling place.

intro.t:
Each dot on this map stands for 250 votes or 250 people who did not vote, scattered around the polling place where they are registered. Blue dots are votes for the Bolsonaro camp, the PL's candidate (Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, Flávio Bolsonaro in 2026), red for Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, amber for people on the roll who did not vote, and grey for votes for the other candidates.

What follows shows where the vote moved between the first rounds of 2022 and 2026.

overview.t:
Lula's share of the vote fell in 5,468 of Brazil's 5,570 municipalities. In 2022 he won 48.4% of the valid vote in the first round and finished ahead. This year he won 45.2%, and Flávio Bolsonaro came first, with 47.0%.

The drop was largest in the South, in small municipalities and in the most Catholic ones. In the state capitals, Lula's share barely changed. In the Northeast it fell about three percentage points, but he is still ahead. Turnout stayed about the same.

On the maps that follow, each circle is a municipality. The colour shows the change in Lula's share of the valid vote between 2022 and 2026: blue where it fell, red where it rose. The area of each circle shows how many votes that change represents.

The ballot is secret. These maps show how places voted. They cannot show which voters changed their minds.

held.t:
Lula's share held or rose in 102 municipalities, shown here. Most are big cities: Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Fortaleza, Manaus, Recife, Belém, Maceió, Aracaju, Niterói and Santos. Together they cast 12 percent of the valid vote.

Places outside the selection fade; the totals at the top count only the lit ones.

slipped.t: His share fell by up to five points in 2,312 municipalities. They include São Paulo, Salvador, most municipalities of 100,000 to 500,000 residents and much of the Northeast, and they cast 63 percent of the valid vote. Across them, Lula's share went from 48.0 percent to 45.6 percent.

shifted.t: In the other 3,156 municipalities his share fell by more than five points. That is more than half of Brazil's municipalities, but they cast only 26 percent of the valid vote. Most are small municipalities in the interior, the South and the Centre-West. Lula's share there dropped from 50.9 percent to 43.6 percent.

small-towns.h: The smaller the municipality, the bigger the shift
small-towns.t:
The average shift grows steadily as places get smaller, from about one percentage point toward the Bolsonaro camp in the biggest cities to seven in towns under 10,000 residents.

This view is a chart, not a map. Each circle is a municipality: further right, more residents; higher, Lula's share rose; lower, it fell. Its area is the valid votes. The white line joins the average change in each population band, such as the −6.7 in towns under 10,000 residents.

abstention.t:
In 2026, 33.5 million people on the roll did not vote, more than voted for any candidate except the two leaders. Abstention has risen in every presidential first round since 2006, from 16.8 percent to 21.1 percent.

Not all of them were required to vote. By the age estimate, 70 percent of non-voters were aged 18 to 69, for whom voting is compulsory. Another 17 percent were 16 or 17 or aged 70 to 79, for whom it is optional, and 13 percent were 80 or older.

It rose by only 0.1 percentage points from 2022, too little to explain, on its own, the fall in Lula's share. Lula received 3.4 million fewer votes than in 2022, and the Bolsonaro camp 5.0 million more. In the quarter of municipalities with the lowest average income, where Lula is strongest, abstention fell 2.5 points. In the quarter with the highest average income, abstention rose 0.9 points.

Abstention fell across the North and Northeast and rose in the South and South-east, and the two moves cancel out. By income, it fell in the poorest places and rose in the richest.

Here the colour is abstention, not the vote: amber where a larger share of the roll stayed home than in 2022, green where a smaller share did. The chart on the right sets each municipality's income against that change.

chart.title: Abstention, presidential first round (% of the roll)

chart2.title: Who didn't vote in 2026, by age

northeast.h: In the Northeast, Lula's share fell three points, but he still leads
northeast.t: Lula still leads in the Northeast, but his share there fell from 66.8 percent to 63.8 percent, and the Bolsonaro camp's rose 3.9 points. In Salvador his share went from 67.0 percent to 65.3 percent. In Feira de Santana, Bahia's second-largest city, it fell from 61.7 percent to 57.1 percent. In a few capitals, such as Fortaleza and Recife, Lula's share held.

capitals.t:
The circles change here: their size is all valid votes, their colour who led and by how much. The labels give Lula's margin in points, 2022 → 2026.

In the 27 state capitals, Lula's share slipped from 45.5 percent to 44.9 percent. Everywhere else it fell from 49.3 percent to 45.2 percent.

The difference is visible in the Rio metropolitan area. The city and Niterói held. Next door, in the Baixada Fluminense and São Gonçalo, the Bolsonaro camp's share grew. Lula's share in each, 2022 to 2026:

chart.title: Lula's share: capitals vs the rest

goias.h: In Goiás, the state's own candidate
goias.t:
Lula's share fell more in Goiás than in any other state, by 8.5 percentage points. Ronaldo Caiado, a former governor, won 12.3 percent of the valid vote in Goiás.

Here each municipality is shaded by Caiado's share of the vote, brighter where he did better.

south.h: Lula's share fell most in the South
south.t: Lula's share fell more in the South than in any other region, by 5.5 percentage points, and by 6.6 points in Rio Grande do Sul. In Caxias do Sul and its neighbours in the hills of the Serra Gaúcha, Lula's share fell about five points. Abstention in the area also rose.

sp-classes-ac.h: In São Paulo, Lula's share rose in the richest neighbourhoods
sp-classes-ac.t:
Zoomed into the city, each circle is a polling place, not a municipality. Colour and size read as before.

In the city of São Paulo as a whole, Lula's share fell. In its richest neighbourhoods, it rose. At polling places in neighbourhoods where household heads earn more than four minimum wages on average (R$ 4,848 a month, at the 2022 census minimum wage of R$ 1,212), Lula's share rose from 39.6 percent to 41.9 percent. The Bolsonaro camp's share also rose, from 42.0 percent to 45.4 percent. The other candidates' combined share fell from 18.4 percent to 12.7 percent. Abstention rose from 22.2 percent to 23.4 percent.

A neighbourhood here is the census tracts within one kilometre of each polling place, and income is the average of the household heads in those tracts. It is not voters' household income, and it does not match the income bands in election polls.

chart.title: Lula's share in São Paulo, by neighbourhood average income

sp-class-d.h: It also fell in neighbourhoods averaging two to four minimum wages
sp-class-d.t: In neighbourhoods where household heads earn two to four minimum wages on average, Lula's share fell from 47.0 percent to 45.5 percent. The Bolsonaro camp rose from 39.3 percent to 43.4 percent. Abstention went from 21.2 percent to 23.2 percent.

chart.title: Lula's share in São Paulo, by neighbourhood average income

sp-class-e.h: And it fell most in the poorest, up to two minimum wages
sp-class-e.t:
Lula still finished first in the poorest neighbourhoods, where household heads earn up to two minimum wages on average. But his share fell from 58.4 percent to 54.5 percent, and the Bolsonaro camp grew from 30.8 percent to 35.7 percent, its largest gain of the three groups. Abstention rose the most here as well, from 20.2 percent to 23.7 percent.

In the city, Lula's share fell in neighbourhoods averaging under four minimum wages, and most of all in the poorest.

chart.title: Lula's share in São Paulo, by neighbourhood average income

religion.h: Lula's share fell further in the most Catholic municipalities
religion.t:
In the most Catholic quarter of municipalities, where at least 80 percent of residents are Catholic, Lula's share fell 5.3 points, from 66.5 percent to 61.2 percent. These places are mostly small and rural. The Bolsonaro camp rose from 27.7 percent to 33.5 percent, and abstention fell from 20.6 percent to 19.5 percent.

In the least Catholic quarter, mostly big cities, Lula's share fell 2.6 points. The quarter of municipalities with the largest share of evangelicals matched the national drop of 3.3 points.

The data describes places. It does not show how Catholics voted.

chart.title: Lula's share by Catholic share of residents

smaller-candidates.h: Where the other candidates did best
smaller-candidates.t:
This map pools polling places into equal-sized hexagons, brighter where the other candidates' combined share was higher. Hollow hexagons hold fewer than 1,000 votes; zoom in for finer cells. The buttons show each candidate separately.

In polling places that hold about a fifth of all voters, candidates other than Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro won 10 percent or more of the valid vote. Together they took 12.1 percent in these places, compared with 7.8 percent nationally. Most of these polling places are in São Paulo state and in Goiás, Ronaldo Caiado's home state, in neighbourhoods with above-average income. Flávio Bolsonaro led Lula there, 51.0 percent to 36.9 percent.

Augusto Cury, Renan Santos and Caiado won 8.7 million votes combined. A Genial/Quaest poll taken 2–3 October asked their voters how they would vote in a runoff between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro. If the poll's split holds for these voters, about 3.9 million would lean toward Flávio Bolsonaro, 1.6 million toward Lula, and 3.2 million would be undecided or back neither. Brazilians vote again on 25 October, when Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro meet in the runoff.

The poll's runoff split is national, applied here to the vote counts. It was not measured at each polling place.

find.t: Type the name of a municipality to see how its vote changed, compared with the country as a whole.

explore.t: Every view in this story comes from the same map. In Explore you can search for any municipality, compare the two years, split abstention by age and filter by the area around each polling place or by municipality. Share view creates a link to what you are looking at.

sp-income.h: In São Paulo, the poorer the neighbourhood, the bigger the drop
sp-income.t:
Split more finely, the city shows a steady gradient. In the tenth of polling places in the poorest neighbourhoods, averaging 1.3 to 1.7 minimum wages, Lula's share fell 4.6 percentage points. The drop shrinks as income rises and turns into a rise above 3.4 minimum wages. In the tenth in the richest neighbourhoods, above 8.8 minimum wages, his share rose 3.3 points.

Across Brazil the pattern is less steady. Nationally, the largest drops came at polling places in neighbourhoods averaging 1.5 to 2.5 minimum wages, not in the poorest.

chart.title: Change in Lula's share, by neighbourhood average income (percentage points)
chart.note: Ten groups of polling places with equal votes, by the average income of household heads nearby, in minimum wages

sp-vs-brazil.h: Elsewhere, Lula's share fell most in middle-income neighbourhoods
sp-vs-brazil.t:
In the rest of the country, Lula's share fell 3.4 percentage points in the poorest neighbourhoods, averaging under one minimum wage, and 4.7 points in those averaging 1.5 to 2.5 minimum wages. His share rose only above six minimum wages.

The city's line sits above the rest of the country's. In neighbourhoods averaging over two minimum wages, Lula's share in the city was 1.3 to 2.5 points higher than elsewhere at the same income. In the city, his share fell most in the poorest neighbourhoods: 5.6 points.

Most votes are cast where his share fell most. In the rest of the country, about seven in ten valid votes come from polling places in neighbourhoods averaging under 2.5 minimum wages.

The map shows only polling places in neighbourhoods averaging 1.5 to 2.5 minimum wages.

chart.title: Change in Lula's share, by neighbourhood average income (percentage points)
chart.axis: Average income of household heads within 1 km, minimum wages
chart.weight: share of the rest of Brazil's vote

flipped.t:
Lula led in 3,379 municipalities in 2022. In 716 of them, the Bolsonaro camp finished ahead this time. No municipality went the other way.

Most are in Minas Gerais (178), Rio Grande do Sul (134), São Paulo and Paraná (91 each). The largest are Osasco, Ananindeua, Betim, Montes Claros and Barueri. Together these 716 municipalities cast 6.9 percent of the valid vote.

studio.note80: Voting is optional at 70+ and 16–17. 80+ is shown apart: the 2026 roll lists 297,977 voters aged 100 or older, and 99% of that group didn't vote in 2022, so the band probably includes people no longer living. Leaving 80+ out takes them out of the dots and rates. Ages for 2026 are estimated.
